extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric, moral philosophy, and statesmanship; educated readers
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the intellectual virtues, defects, knowledge-registers, and social markers (power, worth, honour) discussed in an early-modern moral-philosophical essay; the page gives standards for judging wit, judgement, discretion, prudence, craft, types of knowledge, and behaviours that honour or dishonour a person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertues INTELLECTUALL (general character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vertue generally, in all sorts of subjects, is somewhat that is valued for eminence; and consisteth in comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtues are qualities prized by comparison; intellectual virtues are abilities of mind praised and desired as 'a Good Witte.' The notion of virtue is comparative and socially valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: Naturall Witte vs Acquired Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: These Vertues are of two sorts; Naturall, and Acquired. Naturall Witte is gotten by Use onely, and Experience; without Method, Culture, or Instruction. Acquired Wit is that gotten by method and instruction (Reason producing the Sciences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural wit arises from habit and experience (no formal method). Acquired wit is reason grounded on right use of speech and scientific method. Different standards apply when judging each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural wit — Celerity of Imagining
rubrics_metrics.description: This NATURALL WITTE consisteth principally in two things; Celerity Of Imagining (that is, swift succession of one thought to another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick associative imagination is a positive trait of natural wit; its absence (slowness) leads to dulness or stupidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural wit — Steddy Direction to some approved end
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural wit also consists in Steddy Direction to some approved end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination must be directed and steady toward a purpose; lack of steadiness produces distracting digressions and a kind of madness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect: Dulnesse (slow imagination)
rubrics_metrics.description: A slow Imagination maketh that Defect, or fault of the mind, which is commonly called DULNESSE, Stupidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slowness of thought undermines wit; contrasted with celerity and steadiness which are virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Wit / Good Fancy (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those that observe similitudes, in case they be such as are but rarely observed by others, are sayd to have a Good Wit; by which, in this occasion, is meant a Good Fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good fancy is the power to spot rare likenesses and produce novel, apt metaphors and rare inventions that please and adorn discourse. Fancy is especially prized in poetry and oratory, but must be used with discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Judgement (Distinguishing/Discerning)
rubrics_metrics.description: They that observe their differences, and dissimilitudes; which is called Distinguishing, and Discerning, and Judging between thing and thing, ... are said to have a Good Judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgement is the capacity to perceive distinctions and to choose appropriately; it is prized in history, demonstration, counsel, and practical affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion (judgement of times, places, persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly in matter of conversation and businesse; wherein, times, places, and persons are to be discerned, this Vertue is called DISCRETION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretion is the application of judgement to social context; it governs what may be spoken and to whom. Without discretion, even clever fancy is taken as a sign of want of wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of Fancy and Judgement (normative rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The former, that is, Fancy, without the help of Judgement, is not commended as a Vertue: but the later which is Judgement, and Discretion, is commended for it selfe, without the help of Fancy. Judgement therefore without Fancy is Wit, but Fancy without Judgement not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer judgement/discretion over mere fancy; fancy must be subordinated to judgement. Fancy alone risks indiscretion and folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Digression (application to an End)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is required also an often application of his thoughts to their End; ... Without Steddinesse, and Direction to some End, a great Fancy is one kind of Madnesse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoughts and imaginations should be frequently applied to an intended end; failure produces long digressions and loss of purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary genre standards — Poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In a good Poem, whether it be Epique, or Dramatique; as also in Sonnets, Epigrams, and other Pieces, both Judgement and Fancy are required: But the Fancy must be more eminent; because they please for the Extravagancy; but ought not to displease by Indiscretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry privileges fancy and invention, but poets must avoid indiscretion (inappropriate subject-matter or diction for audiences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary genre standards — History
rubrics_metrics.description: In a good History, the Judgement must be eminent; because the goodnesse consisteth, in the Method, in the Truth, and in the Choyse of the actions that are most profitable to be known. Fancy has no place, but onely in adorning the stile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical writing demands method, truth, and selection of instructive actions; embellishment is limited to stylistic adornment only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary genre standards — Orations of Praise and Invective
rubrics_metrics.description: In Orations of Prayse, and in Invectives, the Fancy is praedominant; because the designe is not truth, but to Honour or Dishonour; which is done by noble, or by vile comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the rhetorical aim is praise or blame, imaginative comparison and ornament (fancy) are primary tools; judgement suggests relevant circumstances but ornament drives effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary genre standards — Hortatives and Pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: In Hortatives, and Pleadings, as Truth, or Disguise serveth best to the Designe in hand; so is the Judgement, or the Fancy most required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persuasive speeches or pleas require a balance: sometimes truth (judgement) best serves, sometimes strategic disguise (fancy) better serves the purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary genre standards — Demonstration and Counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: In Demonstration, in Councell, and all rigourous search of Truth, Judgement does all; except sometimes the understanding have need to be opened by some apt similitude; and then there is so much use of Fancy. But for Metaphors, they are in this case utterly excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious reasoning and counsel should rely on judgement and exclude metaphors that openly profess deceit; metaphors may be used sparingly for illustration, not as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence (operational standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the thoughts of a man, that has a designe in hand, running over a multitude of things, observes how they conduce to that designe; or what designe they may conduce into; if his observations be such as are not easie, or usuall, This wit of his is called PRUDENCE; and dependeth on much Experience, and Memory of the like things, and their consequences heretofore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence is practiced foresight and judgement founded on experience and memory; valued over mere quickness of thought. Prudence varies by domain and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft (crooked wisdom) vs Prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: To Prudence, if you adde the use of unjust, or dishonest means, ... you have that Crooked Wisdome, which is called CRAFT; which is a signe of Pusillanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft is prudence corrupted by dishonesty; it is morally tainted and marks cowardice. Beware confusing shrewdness with ethical prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired Wit as Reason/Science
rubrics_metrics.description: As for Acquired Wit, (I mean acquired by method and instruction,) there is none but Reason; which is grounded on the right use of Speech; and produceth the Sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquired wit is evaluated by the quality of reasoning and adherence to method and correct use of language; it produces demonstrable sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal role of Passions in differences of Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The causes of this difference of Witts, are in the Passions: ... The Passions that most of all cause the differences of Wit, are principally, the more or lesse Desire of Power, of Riches, of Knowledge, and of Honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intellect and tendencies in light of dominant passions: desire of power (and its offshoots) shapes thought direction, steadiness, and ingenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giddinesse, Dulness, and Madnesse (spectrum of mental states)
rubrics_metrics.description: To have weak Passions, is Dulnesse; to have Passions indifferently for every thing, GIDDINESSE, and Distraction; and to have strong, and more vehement Passions ... is that which men call MADNESSE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify mental deficiency by passion-strength: weak passions produce dulness, indifferent passion produces giddiness, excessive passion produces madness. These have characteristic behaviours (distraction, extravagance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rage (madness from pride or excessive passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride, subjecteth a man to Anger, the excesse whereof, is the Madnesse called RAGE, and FURY. ... excessive desire of Revenge ... becomes Rage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive pride or vehement passions may manifest as rage and destructive behavior; note social consequences (mob violence, persecuting friends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Melancholy (madness from dejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dejection, subjects a man to causelesse fears; which is a Madnesse commonly called MELANCHOLY, apparent also in divers manners; as in haunting of solitudes, and graves; in superstitious behaviour; and in fearing some one, some another particular thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dejection-related madness shows in withdrawal, superstitious acts, and irrational fears; distinguish from passion-driven rage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Speech / Absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: That abuse of words ... is, when men speak such words, as put together, have in them no signification at all; but are fallen upon by some, through misunderstanding ... or from intention to deceive by obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech lacking signification (obscure scholastic jargon or deliberately deceptive verbosity) is a defect akin to madness. Examples include abstruse scholastic passages that lack clear meaning. This is an anti-pattern to be avoided in clear reasoning and address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge types: Fact vs Consequence (History vs Science)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are of KNOWLEDGE two kinds; one is Knowledge Of Fact: the other Knowledge Of The Consequence Of One Affirmation To Another. The Register of Knowledge Of Fact is called History. The later is called Science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims by their epistemic register: witness-quality fact (sense and memory) vs demonstrative scientific knowledge (conditional, logical consequences). Use history for facts and science for reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registers and classification of sciences (taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Registers of Science ... are commonly called Books of Philosophy; whereof the sorts are many, according to the diversity of the Matter; And may be divided ... (table: PHILOSOPHIA PRIMA; GEOMETRY; ARITHMETIQUE; ASTRONOMY; GEOGRAPHY; ENGINEERS; ARCHITECTURE; NAVIGATION; METEOROLOGY; ASTROLOGY; OPTIQUES; MUSIQUE; ETHIQUES; POETRY; RHETORIQUE; LOGIQUE; The Science of JUST and UNJUST; POLITIQUES and CIVILL PHILOSOPHY).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided hierarchical taxonomy to locate and judge specialised sciences: distinguishes first philosophy, mathematics, natural philosophy, arts, ethics, rhetoric, logic, and civil/political philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Power (sources and forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The POWER of a Man ... is his present means, to obtain some future apparent Good. And is either Originall, or Instrumentall. Naturall Power is the eminence of the Faculties of Body, or Mind ... Instrumentall are those Powers ... acquired by these, or by fortune, are means and Instruments to acquire more: as Riches, Reputation, Friends, and the Secret working of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess power in terms of faculties (natural) and instruments (wealth, friends, reputation). Consider social mechanisms that translate qualities into political/social power (offices, titles, arts, eloquence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources that constitute Power (practical markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: For example: To have servants, is Power; To have Friends, is Power; Riches joyned with liberality, is Power; Reputation of power, is Power; Affability is increase of Power; Eloquence is Power because it is seeming Prudence; Forme is Power because it recommendeth men to favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a person's power, examine practical markers (servants, friends, wealth with liberality, reputation, affability, eloquence, form). Note that sciences alone are small power unless publicly recognized; practical arts confer power when applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worth (value of a man)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Value, or WORTH of a man, is as of all other things, his Price; that is to say, so much as would be given for the use of his Power: and therefore is not absolute; but a thing dependant on the need and judgement of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a person's worth contextually: price is determined by buyers' needs and judgment. A person's worth varies by situation (wartime vs peace, context-specific skills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity (public worth assigned by commonwealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The publique worth of a man, which is the Value set on him by the Common-wealth, is that which men commonly call DIGNITY. And this Value ... is understood, by offices of Command, Judicature, publike Employment; or by Names and Titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dignity is an externally conferred public valuation (offices, titles); when evaluating dignity consider formal honors and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to Honour and Dishonour (behavioural indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: To pray to another for aid is to HONOUR; To obey is to Honour; To give great gifts is to Honour; To give little gifts is to Dishonour; To be sedulous in promoting another's good is to Honour; To neglect is to Dishonour; To give place or way is to Honour; To arrogate is to Dishonour; To show love or fear is to Honour; To contemne is to Dishonour; ... To praise is to Honour; To revile or mock is to Dishonour; To believe and trust is to Honour; To distrust is to Dishonour; To hearken to counsel is to Honour; To sleep or talk while he speaks is to Dishonour; To agree with in opinion is to Honour; To dissent is Dishonour; To imitate is to Honour; To employ in counsel is to Honour; To deny employment is Dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate interpersonal and ceremonial behaviour against this checklist: many small actions signal honour or dishonour in social life and law/custom. Context and public expectations determine whether a gesture counts as honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic honours (sovereign-conferred signs of honour)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Common-wealths, where he, or they that have the supreme Authority, can make whatsoever they please, to stand for signes of Honour, there be other Honours. A Soveraigne doth Honour a Subject, with whatsoever Title, or Office, or Employment, or Action, that he himselfe will have taken for a signe of his will to Honour him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-conferred honours are conventional and derive authority from the sovereign's will; evaluate them by their social recognition rather than intrinsic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities that are Honourable vs Dishonourable
rubrics_metrics.description: Honourable is whatsoever possession, action, or quality, is an argument and signe of Power. Good fortune (if lasting), Honourable; Ill fortune, Dishonourable. Riches, are Honourable; Poverty, Dishonourable. Magnanimity, Liberality, Hope, Courage, Confidence, are Honourable; Pusillanimity, Parsimony, Fear, Diffidence, are Dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing character, treat traits that signify power and confidence as honourable; traits signaling weakness or excessive caution diminish honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely Resolution as Honourable (and Irresolution as Dishonourable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely Resolution, or determination of what a man is to do, is Honourable ... And Irresolution, Dishonourable; as a signe of too much valuing of little impediments, and little advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate decision-making: prompt, decisive action (after reasonable weighing) is honourable, whereas delay beyond what the situation permits signals pusillanimity and dishonour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech and action from Experience, Science, Discretion, or Wit are Honourable
rubrics_metrics.description: All Actions, and Speeches, that proceed, or seem to proceed from much Experience, Science, Discretion, or Wit, are Honourable; For all these are Powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess social esteem: competence, wisdom, and prudence in words and deeds increase honour. Performance that displays these qualities should be rewarded with respect.
